Create one complete, standalone 3D humanoid character from the supplied brief. Choose the art style yourself. Realistic, stylized and other coherent interpretations are welcome; no particular visual style is preferred or prescribed.

Deliver the finished character as a self-contained GLB. Embed any textures used so the asset does not depend on external image files or remote URLs. The complete character must be inspectable from the front, sides, back and above, with a modeled head, torso, arms, hands, legs and feet. Finish the asset as a whole rather than as a single-view presentation.

Use a neutral A-pose or T-pose with clear separation between the arms and torso and between the legs. The pose should make the character easy to inspect and prepare for later rigging. Express personality through the design, proportions, face and details rather than through an action pose.

Prepare the asset for a later rigging pass: keep the body parts anatomically coherent within your chosen style, avoid accidental fusions between limbs and adjacent clothing, and make the major joints identifiable. A riggable intention is not a claim that untested deformation will work perfectly. A skeleton, skin weights and animations are not required and do not earn credit in this benchmark; focus on the static character. If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Alongside the GLB, provide a short handoff identifying the file, your chosen art direction and any known limitations. Keep the final asset self-contained regardless of how it was made.

TIME LIMIT AND RUN HANDOFF

You have a hard maximum of one hour per character, measured from your actual implementation start. Record that start timestamp and the deadline exactly one hour later before beginning implementation. The hour includes asset creation, tool use, troubleshooting, checking the exported asset and final fixes. Ordinary work and tool waits do not pause the clock. Stop all implementation and asset editing by the deadline, even if the result is incomplete. Record your actual stop timestamp, disclose any interruptions and report unfinished work honestly. Do not replace actual timing evidence with an estimate.

Work independently through the attempt without mid-run coaching messages. Make your own creative and technical decisions within the brief and the existing permissions. If an action needs approval, pause that action and report the blocker; continue other permitted work within the same running time limit.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Your final handoff must identify the GLB file and include the actual implementation-start timestamp, one-hour deadline and actual stop timestamp, with the time zone stated. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Mara Vale, a 67-year-old woman who spent most of her working life maintaining a small rural railway stop. Passenger service ended years ago, but she still clears the drains and repairs what she can. She knows which repairs matter and which only make a place look busy. Her ambition is to keep the old station useful to local walkers without turning it into a monument to her own past.

Mara is short and solidly built, with a broad torso, strong forearms and an age-softened face. She moves deliberately and has the settled physical confidence of someone who has spent decades carrying, lifting and working outdoors. She is particular about promises, fond of very dry jokes and more comfortable teaching someone a task than accepting their sympathy. She has begun letting a younger volunteer make decisions, though she finds this harder than the heavy work.

Give her a specific, lived-in identity rather than a generic elderly worker. Her practical habits and attachment to useful things should inform your design, while leaving room for pride, humor and personal taste. Choose how those qualities appear; no particular garment, tool or keepsake is required.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Farid Mansour, a 68-year-old Arab man who is an astronomer and a maker of precision instruments. He has spent decades observing the sky and building, repairing and calibrating the tools he relies on. An unusual measurement now occupies his attention: he wants to discover whether it reveals something new or exposes a fault in his own instrument. He would rather find his mistake than defend a result nobody else can reproduce.

Farid is tall and lean, with an aged face and careful hands. His bearing is patient and exacting, but his dry, mischievous humor keeps him from seeming remote or solemn. Give him the particular physical presence of a person whose working life combines close observation, delicate manual work and long concentration.

Make him a specific person rather than a generic wise old man. His Arab identity is required; no religious affiliation is specified. You choose his clothing, materials, palette and art style. Express his character through his face, proportions and design rather than relying on a telescope, written labels or a surrounding environment.

BENCHMARK PURPOSE AND GRADING CRITERIA — DRAFT V2

This is a static 3D character benchmark. The host will display your exported asset in a shared neutral inspection studio with camera and lighting controls. Different attempts at the same character brief will be compared side by side. Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

1. Character interpretation — 30 points
- Fidelity to the stated identity, age, physical presence and temperament: 15.
- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

Realism is not inherently better than stylization. Extra polygons, textures or accessories earn no credit by themselves. There is no arbitrary polygon cap or all-quad requirement. A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. The host will record any viewer limitation separately from an asset defect. An asset that cannot be opened cannot receive a visual judgment; retain its failure record without inventing a score.

These criteria are being introduced for this prompt version. Earlier attempts remain associated with the instructions they actually received.

sourceDocuments.text:
Create one complete, standalone 3D humanoid character from the supplied brief. Choose the art style yourself. Realistic, stylized and other coherent interpretations are welcome; no particular visual style is preferred or prescribed.

Deliver the finished character as a self-contained GLB. Embed any textures used so the asset does not depend on external image files or remote URLs. The complete character must be inspectable from the front, sides, back and above, with a modeled head, torso, arms, hands, legs and feet. Finish the asset as a whole rather than as a single-view presentation.

Use a neutral A-pose or T-pose with clear separation between the arms and torso and between the legs. The pose should make the character easy to inspect and prepare for later rigging. Express personality through the design, proportions, face and details rather than through an action pose.

Prepare the asset for a later rigging pass: keep the body parts anatomically coherent within your chosen style, avoid accidental fusions between limbs and adjacent clothing, and make the major joints identifiable. A riggable intention is not a claim that untested deformation will work perfectly. A skeleton, skin weights and animations are not required and do not earn credit in this benchmark; focus on the static character. If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Alongside the GLB, provide a short handoff identifying the file, your chosen art direction and any known limitations. Keep the final asset self-contained regardless of how it was made.

TIME LIMIT AND RUN HANDOFF

You have a hard maximum of one hour per character, measured from your actual implementation start. Record that start timestamp and the deadline exactly one hour later before beginning implementation. The hour includes asset creation, tool use, troubleshooting, checking the exported asset and final fixes. Ordinary work and tool waits do not pause the clock. Stop all implementation and asset editing by the deadline, even if the result is incomplete. Record your actual stop timestamp, disclose any interruptions and report unfinished work honestly. Do not replace actual timing evidence with an estimate.

Work independently through the attempt without mid-run coaching messages. Make your own creative and technical decisions within the brief and the existing permissions. If an action needs approval, pause that action and report the blocker; continue other permitted work within the same running time limit.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Your final handoff must identify the GLB file and include the actual implementation-start timestamp, one-hour deadline and actual stop timestamp, with the time zone stated. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Noor Adebayo, a 22-year-old woman who surveys footpaths along a windy coast. She grew up walking those paths and now has to decide which damaged routes can be repaired and which should be allowed to disappear. She is energetic and direct, enjoys competition, and dislikes admitting that a familiar place has changed. Her ambition is to make a reliable new map without pretending that every route can be saved.

Noor is short and compact, with an athletic build, strong thighs and calves, a narrow waist and sturdy shoulders. Her youthful face is broad through the cheekbones, with alert eyes, a slightly uneven smile and a small healed notch through one eyebrow. Her hair has a close-cut side and a fuller crown of tightly curled hair. Keep her adult proportions and individual facial character clear within the art style you choose.

Design a specific person who spends long days outside, rather than a generic adventurer. Her clothes must include at least two visible layers with different material character, such as a thin weather shell and a heavier woven or knitted garment; you choose the actual garments, palette and construction. Small personal accessories are welcome but optional. Let confidence, impatience and attachment to home appear in her face, proportions and practical design. Keep her face, hands and major joints readily inspectable in the required neutral pose; do not use a map, landscape or action pose to carry the characterization.

BENCHMARK PURPOSE AND GRADING CRITERIA — DRAFT V2

This is a static 3D character benchmark. The host will display your exported asset in a shared neutral inspection studio with camera and lighting controls. Different attempts at the same character brief will be compared side by side. Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

1. Character interpretation — 30 points
- Fidelity to the stated identity, age, physical presence and temperament: 15.
- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

Realism is not inherently better than stylization. Extra polygons, textures or accessories earn no credit by themselves. There is no arbitrary polygon cap or all-quad requirement. A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. The host will record any viewer limitation separately from an asset defect. An asset that cannot be opened cannot receive a visual judgment; retain its failure record without inventing a score.

These criteria are being introduced for this prompt version. Earlier attempts remain associated with the instructions they actually received.

If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Alongside the GLB, provide a short handoff identifying the file, your chosen art direction and any known limitations. Keep the final asset self-contained regardless of how it was made.

TIME LIMIT AND RUN HANDOFF

You have a hard maximum of one hour per character, measured from your actual implementation start. Record that start timestamp and the deadline exactly one hour later before beginning implementation. The hour includes asset creation, tool use, troubleshooting, checking the exported asset and final fixes. Ordinary work and tool waits do not pause the clock. Stop all implementation and asset editing by the deadline, even if the result is incomplete. Record your actual stop timestamp, disclose any interruptions and report unfinished work honestly. Do not replace actual timing evidence with an estimate.

Work independently through the attempt without mid-run coaching messages. Make your own creative and technical decisions within the brief and the existing permissions. If an action needs approval, pause that action and report the blocker; continue other permitted work within the same running time limit.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Your final handoff must identify the GLB file and include the actual implementation-start timestamp, one-hour deadline and actual stop timestamp, with the time zone stated. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Noor Adebayo, a 22-year-old woman who surveys footpaths along a windy coast. She grew up walking those paths and now has to decide which damaged routes can be repaired and which should be allowed to disappear. She is energetic and direct, enjoys competition, and dislikes admitting that a familiar place has changed. Her ambition is to make a reliable new map without pretending that every route can be saved.

Noor is short and compact, with an athletic build, strong thighs and calves, a narrow waist and sturdy shoulders. Her youthful face is broad through the cheekbones, with alert eyes, a slightly uneven smile and a small healed notch through one eyebrow. Her hair has a close-cut side and a fuller crown of tightly curled hair. Keep her adult proportions and individual facial character clear within the art style you choose.

Design a specific person who spends long days outside, rather than a generic adventurer. Her clothes must include at least two visible layers with different material character, such as a thin weather shell and a heavier woven or knitted garment; you choose the actual garments, palette and construction. Small personal accessories are welcome but optional. Let confidence, impatience and attachment to home appear in her face, proportions and practical design. Keep her face, hands and major joints readily inspectable in the required neutral pose; do not use a map, landscape or action pose to carry the characterization.

BENCHMARK PURPOSE AND GRADING CRITERIA — DRAFT V2

This is a static 3D character benchmark. The host will display your exported asset in a shared neutral inspection studio with camera and lighting controls. Different attempts at the same character brief will be compared side by side. Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

1. Character interpretation — 30 points
- Fidelity to the stated identity, age, physical presence and temperament: 15.
- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

Realism is not inherently better than stylization. Extra polygons, textures or accessories earn no credit by themselves. There is no arbitrary polygon cap or all-quad requirement. A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. The host will record any viewer limitation separately from an asset defect. An asset that cannot be opened cannot receive a visual judgment; retain its failure record without inventing a score.

These criteria are being introduced for this prompt version. Earlier attempts remain associated with the instructions they actually received.

Work only in your own fresh workspace and create your own character independently. Do not read or reuse other benchmark entrants or other project assets. Do not invoke other models or subagents. Do not publish or start another task. Do not launch/control a browser, Playwright, native UI, mouse or keyboard, or start preview servers. No GPU/performance benchmarks on the user's computer. Create one complete, standalone 3D humanoid character from the supplied brief. Choose the art style yourself. Realistic, stylized and other coherent interpretations are welcome; no particular visual style is preferred or prescribed.

Deliver the finished character as a self-contained GLB. Embed any textures used so the asset does not depend on external image files or remote URLs. The complete character must be inspectable from the front, sides, back and above, with a modeled head, torso, arms, hands, legs and feet. Finish the asset as a whole rather than as a single-view presentation.

Use a neutral A-pose or T-pose with clear separation between the arms and torso and between the legs. The pose should make the character easy to inspect and prepare for later rigging. Express personality through the design, proportions, face and details rather than through an action pose.

Prepare the asset for a later rigging pass: keep the body parts anatomically coherent within your chosen style, avoid accidental fusions between limbs and adjacent clothing, and make the major joints identifiable. A riggable intention is not a claim that untested deformation will work perfectly. A skeleton, skin weights and animations are not required and do not earn credit in this benchmark; focus on the static character. If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Alongside the GLB, provide a short handoff identifying the file, your chosen art direction and any known limitations. Keep the final asset self-contained regardless of how it was made.

TIME LIMIT AND RUN HANDOFF

You have a hard maximum of one hour per character, measured from your actual implementation start. Record that start timestamp and the deadline exactly one hour later before beginning implementation. The hour includes asset creation, tool use, troubleshooting, checking the exported asset and final fixes. Ordinary work and tool waits do not pause the clock. Stop all implementation and asset editing by the deadline, even if the result is incomplete. Record your actual stop timestamp, disclose any interruptions and report unfinished work honestly. Do not replace actual timing evidence with an estimate.

Work independently through the attempt without mid-run coaching messages. Make your own creative and technical decisions within the brief and the existing permissions. If an action needs approval, pause that action and report the blocker; continue other permitted work within the same running time limit.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Your final handoff must identify the GLB file and include the actual implementation-start timestamp, one-hour deadline and actual stop timestamp, with the time zone stated. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Elena Varga, a 49-year-old woman who conserves costumes for a small touring theatre. She is patient with objects and impatient with excuses, enjoys understated theatrical jokes, and wants to teach an apprentice how to make decisions rather than merely copy her technique.

sourceDocuments.text:
Create one complete, standalone 3D humanoid character from the supplied brief. Choose the art style yourself. Realistic, stylized and other coherent interpretations are welcome; no particular visual style is preferred or prescribed.

Deliver the finished character as a self-contained GLB. Embed any textures used so the asset does not depend on external image files or remote URLs. The complete character must be inspectable from the front, sides, back and above, with a modeled head, torso, arms, hands, legs and feet. Finish the asset as a whole rather than as a single-view presentation.

Use a neutral A-pose or T-pose with clear separation between the arms and torso and between the legs. The pose should make the character easy to inspect and prepare for later rigging. Express personality through the design, proportions, face and details rather than through an action pose.

Prepare the asset for a later rigging pass: keep the body parts anatomically coherent within your chosen style, avoid accidental fusions between limbs and adjacent clothing, and make the major joints identifiable. A riggable intention is not a claim that untested deformation will work perfectly. A skeleton, skin weights and animations are not required and do not earn credit in this benchmark; focus on the static character. If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Alongside the GLB, provide a short handoff identifying the file, your chosen art direction and any known limitations. Keep the final asset self-contained regardless of how it was made.

TIME LIMIT AND RUN HANDOFF

You have a hard maximum of one hour per character, measured from your actual implementation start. Record that start timestamp and the deadline exactly one hour later before beginning implementation. The hour includes asset creation, tool use, troubleshooting, checking the exported asset and final fixes. Ordinary work and tool waits do not pause the clock. Stop all implementation and asset editing by the deadline, even if the result is incomplete. Record your actual stop timestamp, disclose any interruptions and report unfinished work honestly. Do not replace actual timing evidence with an estimate.

Work independently through the attempt without mid-run coaching messages. Make your own creative and technical decisions within the brief and the existing permissions. If an action needs approval, pause that action and report the blocker; continue other permitted work within the same running time limit.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Your final handoff must identify the GLB file and include the actual implementation-start timestamp, one-hour deadline and actual stop timestamp, with the time zone stated. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Elena Varga, a 49-year-old woman who conserves costumes for a small touring theatre. She can make an old garment survive another season without making its repair conspicuous, but she has recently been asked to preserve a costume she once designed badly. She is patient with objects and impatient with excuses, enjoys understated theatrical jokes, and wants to teach an apprentice how to make decisions rather than merely copy her technique.

Elena is tall and broad-shouldered, with long arms, a substantial soft middle and large capable hands. Her face is long and angular, with hooded eyes, visible midlife creases and an asymmetrical, restrained smile. She has thick dark hair threaded with silver, gathered into a practical loose twist with a few escaping strands. Express her age and physical presence without turning her into either a youthful fashion model or a frail elderly figure.

Give her a coherent personal outfit rather than a stage costume or a collection of sewing tools. The design must visibly distinguish woven fabric, supple leather and a small amount of metal through form and material treatment; you choose which garments or compact accessories provide them. Include some intentional wear or repair that reflects her taste without relying on readable labels. Her face, hair, layered silhouette and hands should remain the focal points. Preserve the required neutral pose and clear limb separation, and leave any needles, scissors, furniture or surrounding workshop out of the character asset.

BENCHMARK PURPOSE AND GRADING CRITERIA — DRAFT V2

This is a static 3D character benchmark. The host will display your exported asset in a shared neutral inspection studio with camera and lighting controls. Different attempts at the same character brief will be compared side by side. Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

1. Character interpretation — 30 points
- Fidelity to the stated identity, age, physical presence and temperament: 15.
- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

Realism is not inherently better than stylization. Extra polygons, textures or accessories earn no credit by themselves. There is no arbitrary polygon cap or all-quad requirement. A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. The host will record any viewer limitation separately from an asset defect. An asset that cannot be opened cannot receive a visual judgment; retain its failure record without inventing a score.

These criteria are being introduced for this prompt version. Earlier attempts remain associated with the instructions they actually received.

INITIAL EXECUTION CONSTRAINTS
Work only in your own fresh workspace and create your own character independently. Do not read or reuse other benchmark entrants or other project assets. Do not invoke other models or subagents. Do not publish or start another task. Do not launch/control a browser, Playwright, native UI, mouse or keyboard, or start preview servers. No GPU/performance benchmarks on the user's computer. Headless asset generation and lightweight non-browser asset/export checks are permitted. Disclose visual/interactive/deformation checks not performed. Use available reputable tools within existing permissions; any blocked action stays blocked. Before your final receipt, stop all workspace-owned background/test processes and verify cleanup. Preserve the final self-contained GLB and generation source with timing, actual checks and limitations. Requested model: recorded in the launch metadata; reasoning XHIGH. Disclose if serving backend is not independently exposed. The parent will send no mid-run messages. Use the grading criteria stated above.

All four models receive the same shared launch text. Use this fresh task's own workspace for all creation and artifacts. Record actual implementation start and exact one-hour deadline before implementation; setup, waiting for launch, or coordination before implementation is not the asset clock. Preserve the shared prompt, generation source, final self-contained GLB, actual timing/stop receipt, checks, limitations and hashes. Included Codex only: no purchases, paid APIs, installs, credentials, account/reset/settings or access changes. No prior entrants, other project assets, subagents/models, publication, external messages, browser/native UI, preview servers, GPU or performance benchmarks. Headless creation and lightweight CPU checks only. Report actual final artifact paths so the coordinator can collect them. Do not claim independently verified serving identity unless exposed.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Your final handoff must identify the GLB file and include the actual implementation-start timestamp, one-hour deadline and actual stop timestamp, with the time zone stated. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Milo Chen, an 11-year-old boy who makes small handmade field guides to the overlooked wildlife of his city. He patiently watches puddles and weeds, then rushes through his drawings because he wants to show someone what he found. He is proud of remembering details that adults miss and is learning that being corrected does not spoil a discovery. His current ambition is to finish a guide that a younger child could use without his help.

Milo is small for his age, with a slight build, narrow shoulders, a softly rounded youthful face and an unmistakably childlike relationship between head, torso, hands and limbs. He has short, dense, tousled hair with one stubborn lifted section, wide attentive eyes and a tentative lopsided smile. His hands and feet should feel anatomically coherent for a child within your chosen art style, rather than being scaled versions of an adult body.

Design ordinary, age-appropriate clothing that can handle damp weather and sitting on low walls. Include two visible clothing layers and one modest personal detail that suggests his own taste; you choose the garments, colors, textures and detail. Show everyday wear without making him look neglected. Convey curiosity and the tension between patience and haste through his face and design, not an action pose. Keep the required neutral A-pose or T-pose, visible hands and clear joints. A book, drawing, animal, written label or environment is neither required nor a substitute for a finished character.

BENCHMARK PURPOSE AND GRADING CRITERIA — DRAFT V2

This is a static 3D character benchmark. The host will display your exported asset in a shared neutral inspection studio with camera and lighting controls. Different attempts at the same character brief will be compared side by side. Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

1. Character interpretation — 30 points
- Fidelity to the stated identity, age, physical presence and temperament: 15.
- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

Realism is not inherently better than stylization. Extra polygons, textures or accessories earn no credit by themselves. There is no arbitrary polygon cap or all-quad requirement. A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. The host will record any viewer limitation separately from an asset defect. An asset that cannot be opened cannot receive a visual judgment; retain its failure record without inventing a score.

A small marigold lightning appliqué on his sleeve is his personal detail. The static A-pose leaves the hands and limbs visible. There are no props, environment, lights or camera.

Create one complete, standalone 3D humanoid character from the supplied brief. Choose the art style yourself. Realistic, stylized and other coherent interpretations are welcome; no particular visual style is preferred or prescribed.

Deliver the finished character as a self-contained GLB. Embed any textures used so the asset does not depend on external image files or remote URLs. The complete character must be inspectable from the front, sides, back and above, with a modeled head, torso, arms, hands, legs and feet. Finish the asset as a whole rather than as a single-view presentation.

Use a neutral A-pose or T-pose with clear separation between the arms and torso and between the legs. The pose should make the character easy to inspect and prepare for later rigging. Express personality through the design, proportions, face and details rather than through an action pose.

Prepare the asset for a later rigging pass: keep the body parts anatomically coherent within your chosen style, avoid accidental fusions between limbs and adjacent clothing, and make the major joints identifiable. A riggable intention is not a claim that untested deformation will work perfectly. A skeleton, skin weights and animations are not required and do not earn credit in this benchmark; focus on the static character. If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Alongside the GLB, provide a short handoff identifying the file, your chosen art direction and any known limitations. Keep the final asset self-contained regardless of how it was made.

TIME LIMIT AND RUN HANDOFF

You have a hard maximum of one hour per character, measured from your actual implementation start. Record that start timestamp and the deadline exactly one hour later before beginning implementation. The hour includes asset creation, tool use, troubleshooting, checking the exported asset and final fixes. Ordinary work and tool waits do not pause the clock. Stop all implementation and asset editing by the deadline, even if the result is incomplete. Record your actual stop timestamp, disclose any interruptions and report unfinished work honestly. Do not replace actual timing evidence with an estimate.

Work independently through the attempt without mid-run coaching messages. Make your own creative and technical decisions within the brief and the existing permissions. If an action needs approval, pause that action and report the blocker; continue other permitted work within the same running time limit.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Your final handoff must identify the GLB file and include the actual implementation-start timestamp, one-hour deadline and actual stop timestamp, with the time zone stated. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Milo Chen, an 11-year-old boy who makes small handmade field guides to the overlooked wildlife of his city. He patiently watches puddles and weeds, then rushes through his drawings because he wants to show someone what he found. He is proud of remembering details that adults miss and is learning that being corrected does not spoil a discovery. His current ambition is to finish a guide that a younger child could use without his help.

Milo is small for his age, with a slight build, narrow shoulders, a softly rounded youthful face and an unmistakably childlike relationship between head, torso, hands and limbs. He has short, dense, tousled hair with one stubborn lifted section, wide attentive eyes and a tentative lopsided smile. His hands and feet should feel anatomically coherent for a child within your chosen art style, rather than being scaled versions of an adult body.

Design ordinary, age-appropriate clothing that can handle damp weather and sitting on low walls. Include two visible clothing layers and one modest personal detail that suggests his own taste; you choose the garments, colors, textures and detail. Show everyday wear without making him look neglected. Convey curiosity and the tension between patience and haste through his face and design, not an action pose. Keep the required neutral A-pose or T-pose, visible hands and clear joints. A book, drawing, animal, written label or environment is neither required nor a substitute for a finished character.

BENCHMARK PURPOSE AND GRADING CRITERIA — DRAFT V2

This is a static 3D character benchmark. The host will display your exported asset in a shared neutral inspection studio with camera and lighting controls. Different attempts at the same character brief will be compared side by side. Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

1. Character interpretation — 30 points
- Fidelity to the stated identity, age, physical presence and temperament: 15.
- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

Realism is not inherently better than stylization. Extra polygons, textures or accessories earn no credit by themselves. There is no arbitrary polygon cap or all-quad requirement. A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. The host will record any viewer limitation separately from an asset defect. An asset that cannot be opened cannot receive a visual judgment; retain its failure record without inventing a score.

These criteria are being introduced for this prompt version. Earlier attempts remain associated with the instructions they actually received.

INITIAL EXECUTION CONSTRAINTS
Work only in your own fresh workspace and create your own character independently. Do not read or reuse other benchmark entrants or other project assets. Do not invoke other models or subagents. Do not publish or start another task. Do not launch/control a browser, Playwright, native UI, mouse or keyboard, or start preview servers. No GPU/performance benchmarks on the user's computer. Headless asset generation and lightweight non-browser asset/export checks are permitted. Disclose visual/interactive/deformation checks not performed. Use available reputable tools within existing permissions; any blocked action stays blocked. Before your final receipt, stop all workspace-owned background/test processes and verify cleanup. Preserve the final self-contained GLB and generation source with timing, actual checks and limitations. Requested model: recorded in the launch metadata; reasoning XHIGH. Disclose if serving backend is not independently exposed. The parent will send no mid-run messages. Use the grading criteria stated above.

sourceDocuments.text:
Create one complete, standalone 3D humanoid character from the supplied brief. Choose the art style yourself. Realistic, stylized and other coherent interpretations are welcome; no particular visual style is preferred or prescribed.

Deliver the finished character as a self-contained GLB. Embed any textures used so the asset does not depend on external image files or remote URLs. The complete character must be inspectable from the front, sides, back and above, with a modeled head, torso, arms, hands, legs and feet. Finish the asset as a whole rather than as a single-view presentation.

Use a neutral A-pose or T-pose with clear separation between the arms and torso and between the legs. The pose should make the character easy to inspect and prepare for later rigging. Express personality through the design, proportions, face and details rather than through an action pose.

Prepare the asset for a later rigging pass: keep the body parts anatomically coherent within your chosen style, avoid accidental fusions between limbs and adjacent clothing, and make the major joints identifiable. A riggable intention is not a claim that untested deformation will work perfectly. A skeleton, skin weights and animations are not required and do not earn credit in this benchmark; focus on the static character. If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Alongside the GLB, provide a short handoff identifying the file, your chosen art direction and any known limitations. Keep the final asset self-contained regardless of how it was made.

TIME LIMIT AND RUN HANDOFF

You have a hard maximum of one hour per character, measured from your actual implementation start. Record that start timestamp and the deadline exactly one hour later before beginning implementation. The hour includes asset creation, tool use, troubleshooting, checking the exported asset and final fixes. Ordinary work and tool waits do not pause the clock. Stop all implementation and asset editing by the deadline, even if the result is incomplete. Record your actual stop timestamp, disclose any interruptions and report unfinished work honestly. Do not replace actual timing evidence with an estimate.

Work independently through the attempt without mid-run coaching messages. Make your own creative and technical decisions within the brief and the existing permissions. If an action needs approval, pause that action and report the blocker; continue other permitted work within the same running time limit.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Your final handoff must identify the GLB file and include the actual implementation-start timestamp, one-hour deadline and actual stop timestamp, with the time zone stated. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Milo Chen, an 11-year-old boy who makes small handmade field guides to the overlooked wildlife of his city. He patiently watches puddles and weeds, then rushes through his drawings because he wants to show someone what he found. He is proud of remembering details that adults miss and is learning that being corrected does not spoil a discovery. His current ambition is to finish a guide that a younger child could use without his help.

Milo is small for his age, with a slight build, narrow shoulders, a softly rounded youthful face and an unmistakably childlike relationship between head, torso, hands and limbs. He has short, dense, tousled hair with one stubborn lifted section, wide attentive eyes and a tentative lopsided smile. His hands and feet should feel anatomically coherent for a child within your chosen art style, rather than being scaled versions of an adult body.

Design ordinary, age-appropriate clothing that can handle damp weather and sitting on low walls. Include two visible clothing layers and one modest personal detail that suggests his own taste; you choose the garments, colors, textures and detail. Show everyday wear without making him look neglected. Convey curiosity and the tension between patience and haste through his face and design, not an action pose. Keep the required neutral A-pose or T-pose, visible hands and clear joints. A book, drawing, animal, written label or environment is neither required nor a substitute for a finished character.

BENCHMARK PURPOSE AND GRADING CRITERIA — DRAFT V2

This is a static 3D character benchmark. The host will display your exported asset in a shared neutral inspection studio with camera and lighting controls. Different attempts at the same character brief will be compared side by side. Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

1. Character interpretation — 30 points
- Fidelity to the stated identity, age, physical presence and temperament: 15.
- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

Realism is not inherently better than stylization. Extra polygons, textures or accessories earn no credit by themselves. There is no arbitrary polygon cap or all-quad requirement. A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. The host will record any viewer limitation separately from an asset defect. An asset that cannot be opened cannot receive a visual judgment; retain its failure record without inventing a score.

These criteria are being introduced for this prompt version. Earlier attempts remain associated with the instructions they actually received.

INITIAL EXECUTION CONSTRAINTS

Work only in your own fresh workspace and create your own character independently. Do not read or reuse other benchmark entrants or other project assets. Do not invoke other models or subagents. Do not publish or start another task. Do not launch/control a browser, Playwright, native UI, mouse or keyboard, or start preview servers. No GPU/performance benchmarks on the user's computer. Headless asset generation and lightweight non-browser asset/export checks are permitted. Disclose visual/interactive/deformation checks not performed. Use available reputable tools within existing permissions; any blocked action stays blocked. Before your final receipt, stop all workspace-owned background/test processes and verify cleanup. Preserve the final self-contained GLB and generation source with timing, actual checks and limitations. Requested model: recorded in the launch metadata; reasoning XHIGH. Disclose if serving backend is not independently exposed. The parent will send no mid-run messages. Use the grading criteria stated above.

RUN METADATA

All four models receive the same shared launch text. Use this fresh task's own workspace for all creation and artifacts. Create one complete, standalone 3D humanoid character from the supplied brief. Choose the art style yourself. Realistic, stylized and other coherent interpretations are welcome; no particular visual style is preferred or prescribed.

Deliver the finished character as a self-contained GLB. Embed any textures used so the asset does not depend on external image files or remote URLs. The complete character must be inspectable from the front, sides, back and above, with a modeled head, torso, arms, hands, legs and feet. Finish the asset as a whole rather than as a single-view presentation.

Use a neutral A-pose or T-pose with clear separation between the arms and torso and between the legs. The pose should make the character easy to inspect and prepare for later rigging. Express personality through the design, proportions, face and details rather than through an action pose.

Prepare the asset for a later rigging pass: keep the body parts anatomically coherent within your chosen style, avoid accidental fusions between limbs and adjacent clothing, and make the major joints identifiable. A riggable intention is not a claim that untested deformation will work perfectly. A skeleton, skin weights and animations are not required and do not earn credit in this benchmark; focus on the static character. If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Alongside the GLB, provide a short handoff identifying the file, your chosen art direction and any known limitations. Keep the final asset self-contained regardless of how it was made.

TIME LIMIT AND RUN HANDOFF

You have a hard maximum of one hour per character, measured from your actual implementation start. Record that start timestamp and the deadline exactly one hour later before beginning implementation. The hour includes asset creation, tool use, troubleshooting, checking the exported asset and final fixes. Ordinary work and tool waits do not pause the clock. Stop all implementation and asset editing by the deadline, even if the result is incomplete. Record your actual stop timestamp, disclose any interruptions and report unfinished work honestly. Do not replace actual timing evidence with an estimate.

Work independently through the attempt without mid-run coaching messages. Make your own creative and technical decisions within the brief and the existing permissions. If an action needs approval, pause that action and report the blocker; continue other permitted work within the same running time limit.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Your final handoff must identify the GLB file and include the actual implementation-start timestamp, one-hour deadline and actual stop timestamp, with the time zone stated. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Milo Chen, an 11-year-old boy who makes small handmade field guides to the overlooked wildlife of his city. He patiently watches puddles and weeds, then rushes through his drawings because he wants to show someone what he found. He is proud of remembering details that adults miss and is learning that being corrected does not spoil a discovery. His current ambition is to finish a guide that a younger child could use without his help.

Milo is small for his age, with a slight build, narrow shoulders, a softly rounded youthful face and an unmistakably childlike relationship between head, torso, hands and limbs. He has short, dense, tousled hair with one stubborn lifted section, wide attentive eyes and a tentative lopsided smile. His hands and feet should feel anatomically coherent for a child within your chosen art style, rather than being scaled versions of an adult body.

Design ordinary, age-appropriate clothing that can handle damp weather and sitting on low walls. Include two visible clothing layers and one modest personal detail that suggests his own taste; you choose the garments, colors, textures and detail. Show everyday wear without making him look neglected. Convey curiosity and the tension between patience and haste through his face and design, not an action pose. Keep the required neutral A-pose or T-pose, visible hands and clear joints. A book, drawing, animal, written label or environment is neither required nor a substitute for a finished character.

BENCHMARK PURPOSE AND GRADING CRITERIA — DRAFT V2

This is a static 3D character benchmark. The host will display your exported asset in a shared neutral inspection studio with camera and lighting controls. Different attempts at the same character brief will be compared side by side. Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

1. Character interpretation — 30 points
- Fidelity to the stated identity, age, physical presence and temperament: 15.
- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

Realism is not inherently better than stylization. Extra polygons, textures or accessories earn no credit by themselves. There is no arbitrary polygon cap or all-quad requirement. A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. The host will record any viewer limitation separately from an asset defect. An asset that cannot be opened cannot receive a visual judgment; retain its failure record without inventing a score.

These criteria are being introduced for this prompt version. Earlier attempts remain associated with the instructions they actually received.

Create one complete, standalone 3D humanoid character from the supplied brief. Choose the art style yourself. Realistic, stylized and other coherent interpretations are welcome; no particular visual style is preferred or prescribed.

Deliver the finished character as a self-contained GLB. Embed any textures used so the asset does not depend on external image files or remote URLs. The complete character must be inspectable from the front, sides, back and above, with a modeled head, torso, arms, hands, legs and feet. Finish the asset as a whole rather than as a single-view presentation.

Use a neutral A-pose or T-pose with clear separation between the arms and torso and between the legs. The pose should make the character easy to inspect and prepare for later rigging. Express personality through the design, proportions, face and details rather than through an action pose.

Prepare the asset for a later rigging pass: keep the body parts anatomically coherent within your chosen style, avoid accidental fusions between limbs and adjacent clothing, and make the major joints identifiable. A riggable intention is not a claim that untested deformation will work perfectly. A skeleton, skin weights and animations are not required and do not earn credit in this benchmark; focus on the static character. If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Alongside the GLB, provide a short handoff identifying the file, your chosen art direction and any known limitations. Keep the final asset self-contained regardless of how it was made.

TIME LIMIT AND RUN HANDOFF

You have a hard maximum of one hour per character, measured from your actual implementation start. Record that start timestamp and the deadline exactly one hour later before beginning implementation. The hour includes asset creation, tool use, troubleshooting, checking the exported asset and final fixes. Ordinary work and tool waits do not pause the clock. Stop all implementation and asset editing by the deadline, even if the result is incomplete. Record your actual stop timestamp, disclose any interruptions and report unfinished work honestly. Do not replace actual timing evidence with an estimate.

Work independently through the attempt without mid-run coaching messages. Make your own creative and technical decisions within the brief and the existing permissions. If an action needs approval, pause that action and report the blocker; continue other permitted work within the same running time limit.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Otto Berg, a 78-year-old man who taught swimming at a neighborhood pool for forty years. The pool has closed for repairs, and he now organizes gentle walking groups so his former pupils keep meeting. He is sociable but never loud, remembers people's small achievements, and quietly fears becoming someone who only tells stories about what he used to do. He wants to learn the names of the new families moving into the neighborhood.

Otto is short and heavyset, with a rounded abdomen, a wide chest, thick ankles and large hands. His aged face has deep smile lines, soft cheeks, a broad nose and a close white mustache. His hair is sparse on top and fuller around the sides. Give him an upright, comfortable neutral stance with coherent knees and shoulders; age should be visible without making him a caricature of frailty.

Choose ordinary clothes that show comfort and some personal pride. Include a soft knitted or brushed fabric and a visibly firmer woven layer, with believable seams and different surface character. Footwear should fit his broad feet and feel chosen for daily walking. One compact personal accessory may hint at his habits, but no swimming equipment, medals, walking aids or environmental objects are required. Let warmth, dignity and a little uncertainty emerge through his face and proportions while preserving clear limb separation and inspectable hands.

BENCHMARK PURPOSE AND GRADING CRITERIA — DRAFT V2

This is a static 3D character benchmark. The host will display your exported asset in a shared neutral inspection studio with camera and lighting controls. Different attempts at the same character brief will be compared side by side. Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

1. Character interpretation — 30 points
- Fidelity to the stated identity, age, physical presence and temperament: 15.
- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

Realism is not inherently better than stylization. Extra polygons, textures or accessories earn no credit by themselves. There is no arbitrary polygon cap or all-quad requirement. A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. An asset that cannot be opened cannot receive a visual judgment; retain its failure record without inventing a score.
