sourceDocuments.text:
Create one complete, standalone 3D humanoid character from the supplied brief. Choose the art style yourself. Realistic, stylized and other coherent interpretations are welcome; no particular visual style is preferred or prescribed.

Deliver the finished character as a self-contained GLB. Embed any textures used so the asset does not depend on external image files or remote URLs. The complete character must be inspectable from the front, sides, back and above, with a modeled head, torso, arms, hands, legs and feet. Finish the asset as a whole rather than as a single-view presentation.

Use a neutral A-pose or T-pose with clear separation between the arms and torso and between the legs. The pose should make the character easy to inspect and prepare for later rigging. Express personality through the design, proportions, face and details rather than through an action pose.

Prepare the asset for a later rigging pass: keep the body parts anatomically coherent within your chosen style, avoid accidental fusions between limbs and adjacent clothing, and make the major joints identifiable. A riggable intention is not a claim that untested deformation will work perfectly. A skeleton, skin weights and animations are not required and do not earn credit in this benchmark; focus on the static character. If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Alongside the GLB, provide a short handoff identifying the file, your chosen art direction and any known limitations. Keep the final asset self-contained regardless of how it was made.

TIME LIMIT AND RUN HANDOFF

You have a hard maximum of one hour per character, measured from your actual implementation start. Record that start timestamp and the deadline exactly one hour later before beginning implementation. The hour includes asset creation, tool use, troubleshooting, checking the exported asset and final fixes. Ordinary work and tool waits do not pause the clock. Stop all implementation and asset editing by the deadline, even if the result is incomplete. Record your actual stop timestamp, disclose any interruptions and report unfinished work honestly. Do not replace actual timing evidence with an estimate.

Work independently through the attempt without mid-run coaching messages. Make your own creative and technical decisions within the brief and the existing permissions. If an action needs approval, pause that action and report the blocker; continue other permitted work within the same running time limit.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Your final handoff must identify the GLB file and include the actual implementation-start timestamp, one-hour deadline and actual stop timestamp, with the time zone stated. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Rafi Haddad, an 18-year-old man apprenticed to a neighborhood shoe repairer. He is proud of learning work that leaves a useful object behind, but he hides his uncertainty by offering to finish jobs too quickly. He has promised to restore a customer's favorite boots without asking his teacher to take over. He is courteous, curious about people's stories and unexpectedly funny when he forgets to impress them.

Rafi is very slender and lanky, with narrow shoulders, long forearms, prominent knees and feet that seem a little large for his frame. His face is long and youthful, with a narrow jaw, a slightly crooked nose, large ears and only faint early facial hair. His thick straight hair falls unevenly across his forehead. Keep him unmistakably a young adult, with coherent but not yet filled-out proportions and carefully modeled hands.

Choose clothes that mix his own taste with the practical needs of messy hand work. Include a worn protective layer over an ordinary soft garment, with distinct material thickness, edges and fastenings. A small repaired or customized detail should feel deliberate rather than random damage. His nervous pride should come through in the face and design while the body remains in the required neutral inspection pose. Do not rely on a held shoe, bench, tools, written labels or a surrounding shop.

BENCHMARK PURPOSE AND GRADING CRITERIA — DRAFT V2

This is a static 3D character benchmark. The host will display your exported asset in a shared neutral inspection studio with camera and lighting controls. Different attempts at the same character brief will be compared side by side. Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

1. Character interpretation — 30 points
- Fidelity to the stated identity, age, physical presence and temperament: 15.
- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

Realism is not inherently better than stylization. Extra polygons, textures or accessories earn no credit by themselves. There is no arbitrary polygon cap or all-quad requirement. A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. The host will record any viewer limitation separately from an asset defect. An asset that cannot be opened cannot receive a visual judgment; retain its failure record without inventing a score.

These criteria are being introduced for this prompt version. Earlier attempts remain associated with the instructions they actually received.

INITIAL EXECUTION CONSTRAINTS
Work only in your own fresh workspace and create your own character independently. Do not read or reuse other benchmark entrants or other project assets. Do not invoke other models or subagents. Do not publish or start another task. Do not launch/control a browser, Playwright, native UI, mouse or keyboard, or start preview servers. No GPU/performance benchmarks on the user's computer. Headless asset generation and lightweight non-browser asset/export checks are permitted. Disclose visual/interactive/deformation checks not performed. Use available reputable tools within existing permissions; any blocked action stays blocked. Before your final receipt, stop all workspace-owned background/test processes and verify cleanup. Preserve the final self-contained GLB and generation source with timing, actual checks and limitations. Requested model: recorded in the launch metadata; reasoning XHIGH. Disclose if serving backend is not independently exposed. The parent will send no mid-run messages. Use the grading criteria stated above.

{

  "promptVersion": "new-brief-v1",
  "sharedContract": "Original CharacterBench static GLB contract; 3600 seconds per attempt",
  "sharedEvaluation": "Unchanged established Farid v2 rubric: interpretation 30, visual execution 45, technical quality/inspectability 25; no invented automatic scores",
  "requestedReasoning": "xhigh",
  "modelCatalogNote": "Latest available collaboration catalog: gpt-6-astra, gpt-6.1-sol, gpt-6.1-terra, gpt-6-luna. A 6.1 Luna variant is not offered; gpt-6-luna is explicitly selected.",
  "prompts": [
    {
      "id": "12-v1",
      "title": "Dalia Okoro",
      "text": "Create one complete, standalone 3D humanoid character from the supplied brief. Choose the art style yourself. Realistic, stylized and other coherent interpretations are welcome; no particular visual style is preferred or prescribed.

Deliver the finished character as a self-contained GLB. Embed any textures used so the asset does not depend on external image files or remote URLs. The complete character must be inspectable from the front, sides, back and above, with a modeled head, torso, arms, hands, legs and feet. Finish the asset as a whole rather than as a single-view presentation.

Use a neutral A-pose or T-pose with clear separation between the arms and torso and between the legs. The pose should make the character easy to inspect and prepare for later rigging. Express personality through the design, proportions, face and details rather than through an action pose.

Prepare the asset for a later rigging pass: keep the body parts anatomically coherent within your chosen style, avoid accidental fusions between limbs and adjacent clothing, and make the major joints identifiable. A riggable intention is not a claim that untested deformation will work perfectly. A skeleton, skin weights and animations are not required and do not earn credit in this benchmark; focus on the static character. If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Alongside the GLB, provide a short handoff identifying the file, your chosen art direction and any known limitations. Keep the final asset self-contained regardless of how it was made.

TIME LIMIT AND RUN HANDOFF

You have a hard maximum of one hour per character, measured from your actual implementation start. Record that start timestamp and the deadline exactly one hour later before beginning implementation. The hour includes asset creation, tool use, troubleshooting, checking the exported asset and final fixes. Ordinary work and tool waits do not pause the clock. Stop all implementation and asset editing by the deadline, even if the result is incomplete. Record your actual stop timestamp, disclose any interruptions and report unfinished work honestly. Do not replace actual timing evidence with an estimate.

Work independently through the attempt without mid-run coaching messages. Make your own creative and technical decisions within the brief and the existing permissions. If an action needs approval, pause that action and report the blocker; continue other permitted work within the same running time limit.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Your final handoff must identify the GLB file and include the actual implementation-start timestamp, one-hour deadline and actual stop timestamp, with the time zone stated. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Dalia Okoro, a 57-year-old Black woman who manages a shared ceramics kiln. She likes precise schedules because they let everyone experiment without ruining a neighbor's work. A successful exhibition has made people treat her as an authority, and she is trying to remain willing to admit when she does not know why a glaze failed. She is generous with practical help, enjoys quiet absurdity and wants the youngest members to stop asking permission for every idea.

Dalia is of average height and very heavyset, with a broad chest, a full abdomen and hips, substantial upper arms and strong hands. Her face is round with pronounced cheekbones, deep brown skin, alert eyes and expressive smile lines. She wears her dense coiled hair mostly gathered in a cloth wrap, with some hair visible at the edges. Model her body as a coherent three-dimensional form from every angle, including the back, rather than treating its fullness as a front silhouette.

Choose an outfit that combines comfort with a clear personal sense of color. Include layered woven cloth and the wrapped fabric around her head, distinguishing their construction, tension and folds. One compact piece of jewelry or another modest personal detail may provide a harder material contrast. Keep her face, hands and joints inspectable; any protective garment should fit her body rather than conceal it entirely. No clay pots, tools, kiln, labels or environment are required, and retain the neutral pose.

BENCHMARK PURPOSE AND GRADING CRITERIA — DRAFT V2

This is a static 3D character benchmark. The host will display your exported asset in a shared neutral inspection studio with camera and lighting controls. Different attempts at the same character brief will be compared side by side. Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

1. Character interpretation — 30 points
- Fidelity to the stated identity, age, physical presence and temperament: 15.
- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

Realism is not inherently better than stylization. Extra polygons, textures or accessories earn no credit by themselves. There is no arbitrary polygon cap or all-quad requirement. A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. The host will record any viewer limitation separately from an asset defect. An asset that cannot be opened cannot receive a visual judgment; retain its failure record without inventing a score.

Create one complete, standalone 3D humanoid character from the supplied brief. Choose the art style yourself. Realistic, stylized and other coherent interpretations are welcome; no particular visual style is preferred or prescribed.

Deliver the finished character as a self-contained GLB. Embed any textures used so the asset does not depend on external image files or remote URLs. The complete character must be inspectable from the front, sides, back and above, with a modeled head, torso, arms, hands, legs and feet. Finish the asset as a whole rather than as a single-view presentation.

Use a neutral A-pose or T-pose with clear separation between the arms and torso and between the legs. The pose should make the character easy to inspect and prepare for later rigging. Express personality through the design, proportions, face and details rather than through an action pose.

Prepare the asset for a later rigging pass: keep the body parts anatomically coherent within your chosen style, avoid accidental fusions between limbs and adjacent clothing, and make the major joints identifiable. A riggable intention is not a claim that untested deformation will work perfectly. A skeleton, skin weights and animations are not required and do not earn credit in this benchmark; focus on the static character. If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Alongside the GLB, provide a short handoff identifying the file, your chosen art direction and any known limitations. Keep the final asset self-contained regardless of how it was made.

TIME LIMIT AND RUN HANDOFF

You have a hard maximum of one hour per character, measured from your actual implementation start. Record that start timestamp and the deadline exactly one hour later before beginning implementation. The hour includes asset creation, tool use, troubleshooting, checking the exported asset and final fixes. Ordinary work and tool waits do not pause the clock. Stop all implementation and asset editing by the deadline, even if the result is incomplete. Record your actual stop timestamp, disclose any interruptions and report unfinished work honestly. Do not replace actual timing evidence with an estimate.

Work independently through the attempt without mid-run coaching messages. Make your own creative and technical decisions within the brief and the existing permissions. If an action needs approval, pause that action and report the blocker; continue other permitted work within the same running time limit.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Your final handoff must identify the GLB file and include the actual implementation-start timestamp, one-hour deadline and actual stop timestamp, with the time zone stated. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Dalia Okoro, a 57-year-old Black woman who manages a shared ceramics kiln. She likes precise schedules because they let everyone experiment without ruining a neighbor's work. A successful exhibition has made people treat her as an authority, and she is trying to remain willing to admit when she does not know why a glaze failed. She is generous with practical help, enjoys quiet absurdity and wants the youngest members to stop asking permission for every idea.

Dalia is of average height and very heavyset, with a broad chest, a full abdomen and hips, substantial upper arms and strong hands. Her face is round with pronounced cheekbones, deep brown skin, alert eyes and expressive smile lines. She wears her dense coiled hair mostly gathered in a cloth wrap, with some hair visible at the edges. Model her body as a coherent three-dimensional form from every angle, including the back, rather than treating its fullness as a front silhouette.

Choose an outfit that combines comfort with a clear personal sense of color. Include layered woven cloth and the wrapped fabric around her head, distinguishing their construction, tension and folds. One compact piece of jewelry or another modest personal detail may provide a harder material contrast. Keep her face, hands and joints inspectable; any protective garment should fit her body rather than conceal it entirely. No clay pots, tools, kiln, labels or environment are required, and retain the neutral pose.

BENCHMARK PURPOSE AND GRADING CRITERIA — DRAFT V2

This is a static 3D character benchmark. The host will display your exported asset in a shared neutral inspection studio with camera and lighting controls. Different attempts at the same character brief will be compared side by side. Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

1. Character interpretation — 30 points
- Fidelity to the stated identity, age, physical presence and temperament: 15.
- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

Realism is not inherently better than stylization. Extra polygons, textures or accessories earn no credit by themselves. There is no arbitrary polygon cap or all-quad requirement. A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. The host will record any viewer limitation separately from an asset defect. An asset that cannot be opened cannot receive a visual judgment; retain its failure record without inventing a score.

Create one complete, standalone 3D humanoid character from the supplied brief. Choose the art style yourself. Realistic, stylized and other coherent interpretations are welcome; no particular visual style is preferred or prescribed.

Deliver the finished character as a self-contained GLB. Embed any textures used so the asset does not depend on external image files or remote URLs. The complete character must be inspectable from the front, sides, back and above, with a modeled head, torso, arms, hands, legs and feet. Finish the asset as a whole rather than as a single-view presentation.

Use a neutral A-pose or T-pose with clear separation between the arms and torso and between the legs. The pose should make the character easy to inspect and prepare for later rigging. Express personality through the design, proportions, face and details rather than through an action pose.

Prepare the asset for a later rigging pass: keep the body parts anatomically coherent within your chosen style, avoid accidental fusions between limbs and adjacent clothing, and make the major joints identifiable. A riggable intention is not a claim that untested deformation will work perfectly. A skeleton, skin weights and animations are not required and do not earn credit in this benchmark; focus on the static character. If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Alongside the GLB, provide a short handoff identifying the file, your chosen art direction and any known limitations. Keep the final asset self-contained regardless of how it was made.

TIME LIMIT AND RUN HANDOFF

You have a hard maximum of one hour per character, measured from your actual implementation start. Record that start timestamp and the deadline exactly one hour later before beginning implementation. The hour includes asset creation, tool use, troubleshooting, checking the exported asset and final fixes. Ordinary work and tool waits do not pause the clock. Stop all implementation and asset editing by the deadline, even if the result is incomplete. Record your actual stop timestamp, disclose any interruptions and report unfinished work honestly. Do not replace actual timing evidence with an estimate.

Work independently through the attempt without mid-run coaching messages. Make your own creative and technical decisions within the brief and the existing permissions. If an action needs approval, pause that action and report the blocker; continue other permitted work within the same running time limit.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Your final handoff must identify the GLB file and include the actual implementation-start timestamp, one-hour deadline and actual stop timestamp, with the time zone stated. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Dalia Okoro, a 57-year-old Black woman who manages a shared ceramics kiln. She likes precise schedules because they let everyone experiment without ruining a neighbor's work. A successful exhibition has made people treat her as an authority, and she is trying to remain willing to admit when she does not know why a glaze failed. She is generous with practical help, enjoys quiet absurdity and wants the youngest members to stop asking permission for every idea.

Dalia is of average height and very heavyset, with a broad chest, a full abdomen and hips, substantial upper arms and strong hands. Her face is round with pronounced cheekbones, deep brown skin, alert eyes and expressive smile lines. She wears her dense coiled hair mostly gathered in a cloth wrap, with some hair visible at the edges. Model her body as a coherent three-dimensional form from every angle, including the back, rather than treating its fullness as a front silhouette.

Choose an outfit that combines comfort with a clear personal sense of color. Include layered woven cloth and the wrapped fabric around her head, distinguishing their construction, tension and folds. One compact piece of jewelry or another modest personal detail may provide a harder material contrast. Keep her face, hands and joints inspectable; any protective garment should fit her body rather than conceal it entirely. No clay pots, tools, kiln, labels or environment are required, and retain the neutral pose.

BENCHMARK PURPOSE AND GRADING CRITERIA — DRAFT V2

This is a static 3D character benchmark. The host will display your exported asset in a shared neutral inspection studio with camera and lighting controls. Different attempts at the same character brief will be compared side by side. Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

1. Character interpretation — 30 points
- Fidelity to the stated identity, age, physical presence and temperament: 15.
- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

Realism is not inherently better than stylization. Extra polygons, textures or accessories earn no credit by themselves. There is no arbitrary polygon cap or all-quad requirement. A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. The host will record any viewer limitation separately from an asset defect. An asset that cannot be opened cannot receive a visual judgment; retain its failure record without inventing a score.

sourceDocuments.text:
Create one complete, standalone 3D humanoid character from the supplied brief. Choose the art style yourself. Realistic, stylized and other coherent interpretations are welcome; no particular visual style is preferred or prescribed.

Deliver the finished character as a self-contained GLB. Embed any textures used so the asset does not depend on external image files or remote URLs. The complete character must be inspectable from the front, sides, back and above, with a modeled head, torso, arms, hands, legs and feet. Finish the asset as a whole rather than as a single-view presentation.

Use a neutral A-pose or T-pose with clear separation between the arms and torso and between the legs. The pose should make the character easy to inspect and prepare for later rigging. Express personality through the design, proportions, face and details rather than through an action pose.

Prepare the asset for a later rigging pass: keep the body parts anatomically coherent within your chosen style, avoid accidental fusions between limbs and adjacent clothing, and make the major joints identifiable. A riggable intention is not a claim that untested deformation will work perfectly. A skeleton, skin weights and animations are not required and do not earn credit in this benchmark; focus on the static character. If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Alongside the GLB, provide a short handoff identifying the file, your chosen art direction and any known limitations. Keep the final asset self-contained regardless of how it was made.

TIME LIMIT AND RUN HANDOFF

You have a hard maximum of one hour per character, measured from your actual implementation start. Record that start timestamp and the deadline exactly one hour later before beginning implementation. The hour includes asset creation, tool use, troubleshooting, checking the exported asset and final fixes. Ordinary work and tool waits do not pause the clock. Stop all implementation and asset editing by the deadline, even if the result is incomplete. Record your actual stop timestamp, disclose any interruptions and report unfinished work honestly. Do not replace actual timing evidence with an estimate.

Work independently through the attempt without mid-run coaching messages. Make your own creative and technical decisions within the brief and the existing permissions. If an action needs approval, pause that action and report the blocker; continue other permitted work within the same running time limit.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Your final handoff must identify the GLB file and include the actual implementation-start timestamp, one-hour deadline and actual stop timestamp, with the time zone stated. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Dalia Okoro, a 57-year-old Black woman who manages a shared ceramics kiln. She likes precise schedules because they let everyone experiment without ruining a neighbor's work. A successful exhibition has made people treat her as an authority, and she is trying to remain willing to admit when she does not know why a glaze failed. She is generous with practical help, enjoys quiet absurdity and wants the youngest members to stop asking permission for every idea.

Dalia is of average height and very heavyset, with a broad chest, a full abdomen and hips, substantial upper arms and strong hands. Her face is round with pronounced cheekbones, deep brown skin, alert eyes and expressive smile lines. She wears her dense coiled hair mostly gathered in a cloth wrap, with some hair visible at the edges. Model her body as a coherent three-dimensional form from every angle, including the back, rather than treating its fullness as a front silhouette.

Choose an outfit that combines comfort with a clear personal sense of color. Include layered woven cloth and the wrapped fabric around her head, distinguishing their construction, tension and folds. One compact piece of jewelry or another modest personal detail may provide a harder material contrast. Keep her face, hands and joints inspectable; any protective garment should fit her body rather than conceal it entirely. No clay pots, tools, kiln, labels or environment are required, and retain the neutral pose.

BENCHMARK PURPOSE AND GRADING CRITERIA — DRAFT V2

This is a static 3D character benchmark. The host will display your exported asset in a shared neutral inspection studio with camera and lighting controls. Different attempts at the same character brief will be compared side by side. Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

1. Character interpretation — 30 points
- Fidelity to the stated identity, age, physical presence and temperament: 15.
- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

Realism is not inherently better than stylization. Extra polygons, textures or accessories earn no credit by themselves. There is no arbitrary polygon cap or all-quad requirement. A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. The host will record any viewer limitation separately from an asset defect. An asset that cannot be opened cannot receive a visual judgment; retain its failure record without inventing a score.

These criteria are being introduced for this prompt version. Earlier attempts remain associated with the instructions they actually received.

INITIAL EXECUTION CONSTRAINTS
Work only in your own fresh workspace and create your own character independently. Do not read or reuse other benchmark entrants or other project assets. Do not invoke other models or subagents. Do not publish or start another task. Do not launch/control a browser, Playwright, native UI, mouse or keyboard, or start preview servers. No GPU/performance benchmarks on the user's computer. Headless asset generation and lightweight non-browser asset/export checks are permitted. Disclose visual/interactive/deformation checks not performed. Use available reputable tools within existing permissions; any blocked action stays blocked. Before your final receipt, stop all workspace-owned background/test processes and verify cleanup. Preserve the final self-contained GLB and generation source with timing, actual checks and limitations. Requested model: recorded in the launch metadata; reasoning XHIGH. Disclose if serving backend is not independently exposed. The parent will send no mid-run messages. Use the grading criteria stated above.

Create one complete, standalone 3D humanoid character from the supplied brief. Choose the art style yourself. Realistic, stylized and other coherent interpretations are welcome; no particular visual style is preferred or prescribed.

Deliver the finished character as a self-contained GLB. Embed any textures used so the asset does not depend on external image files or remote URLs. The complete character must be inspectable from the front, sides, back and above, with a modeled head, torso, arms, hands, legs and feet. Finish the asset as a whole rather than as a single-view presentation.

Use a neutral A-pose or T-pose with clear separation between the arms and torso and between the legs. The pose should make the character easy to inspect and prepare for later rigging. Express personality through the design, proportions, face and details rather than through an action pose.

Prepare the asset for a later rigging pass: keep the body parts anatomically coherent within your chosen style, avoid accidental fusions between limbs and adjacent clothing, and make the major joints identifiable. A riggable intention is not a claim that untested deformation will work perfectly. A skeleton, skin weights and animations are not required and do not earn credit in this benchmark; focus on the static character. If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Sora Kim, a 34-year-old man who plays piano on an overnight ferry. He can repeat a familiar set without seeming bored, but has begun collecting requests because he wants to discover what passengers actually remember about the journey. He is reserved until someone asks a precise question, then becomes unexpectedly animated. He hopes to compose a short piece that sounds like the place he lives without imitating waves or engines.

Sora is of medium height, slender through the shoulders and chest, with fuller hips, long fingers and narrow feet. His face is softly oval with prominent cheekbones, a small chin and slightly tired eyes. His straight dark hair is cut in a deliberate asymmetric bob, tucked behind one ear. Give him a thoughtful, faintly amused expression rather than a vacant mannequin face, and make the hands and hair convincing focal details within the chosen style.

Choose clothing that bridges a casual daytime life and an understated evening job. Include a structured outer layer over draped or finely knitted fabric, with visible distinctions in thickness, folds and edge construction. One small metal accessory may add a point of polish, but keep the overall design personal rather than a performance uniform. The required neutral pose must leave the fingers, torso and leg separation readable. No piano, music sheet, ferry furniture, written notes or surrounding scene is required.

Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. The host will record any viewer limitation separately from an asset defect. Create one complete, standalone 3D humanoid character from the supplied brief. Choose the art style yourself. Realistic, stylized and other coherent interpretations are welcome; no particular visual style is preferred or prescribed.

Deliver the finished character as a self-contained GLB. Embed any textures used so the asset does not depend on external image files or remote URLs. The complete character must be inspectable from the front, sides, back and above, with a modeled head, torso, arms, hands, legs and feet. Finish the asset as a whole rather than as a single-view presentation.

Use a neutral A-pose or T-pose with clear separation between the arms and torso and between the legs. The pose should make the character easy to inspect and prepare for later rigging. Express personality through the design, proportions, face and details rather than through an action pose.

Prepare the asset for a later rigging pass: keep the body parts anatomically coherent within your chosen style, avoid accidental fusions between limbs and adjacent clothing, and make the major joints identifiable. A riggable intention is not a claim that untested deformation will work perfectly. A skeleton, skin weights and animations are not required and do not earn credit in this benchmark; focus on the static character. If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Alongside the GLB, provide a short handoff identifying the file, your chosen art direction and any known limitations. Keep the final asset self-contained regardless of how it was made.

TIME LIMIT AND RUN HANDOFF

You have a hard maximum of one hour per character, measured from your actual implementation start. Record that start timestamp and the deadline exactly one hour later before beginning implementation. The hour includes asset creation, tool use, troubleshooting, checking the exported asset and final fixes. Ordinary work and tool waits do not pause the clock. Stop all implementation and asset editing by the deadline, even if the result is incomplete. Record your actual stop timestamp, disclose any interruptions and report unfinished work honestly. Do not replace actual timing evidence with an estimate.

Work independently through the attempt without mid-run coaching messages. Make your own creative and technical decisions within the brief and the existing permissions. If an action needs approval, pause that action and report the blocker; continue other permitted work within the same running time limit.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Your final handoff must identify the GLB file and include the actual implementation-start timestamp, one-hour deadline and actual stop timestamp, with the time zone stated. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Beatriz Costa, a 42-year-old woman who supervises a volunteer emergency-response team. Away from the uniform, she restores old kites and dislikes being treated as permanently on duty. She is calm when plans fail and restless when nothing needs fixing. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Beatriz Costa, a 42-year-old woman who supervises a volunteer emergency-response team. Away from the uniform, she restores old kites and dislikes being treated as permanently on duty. She is calm when plans fail and restless when nothing needs fixing. She has promised her family that she will let someone else organize the next outing, and is trying to keep that small promise with the seriousness she gives larger ones.

Beatriz is of average height with a muscular, compact build, a broad upper back, strong neck, thick forearms and powerful legs. Her face is square, with a broad nose, dark attentive eyes, sun freckles and a slight crease between the brows. Her curly hair is tied into a short practical ponytail, with a few loose curls at the forehead. Give her a relaxed but alert neutral expression and make the transition from neck to shoulders and arms anatomically coherent.

Design her in everyday clothes that express interests beyond her job. Include a substantial woven garment and a softer layer with clearly different surface treatment, plus one modest personal detail chosen by you. Show how sleeves, hems and footwear fit an athletic body without hiding the major joints. Do not use a uniform, insignia, emergency equipment, a kite or a surrounding scene to explain her. Maintain the required neutral inspection pose and keep both hands and the face unobstructed.

BENCHMARK PURPOSE AND GRADING CRITERIA — DRAFT V2

This is a static 3D character benchmark. The host will display your exported asset in a shared neutral inspection studio with camera and lighting controls. Different attempts at the same character brief will be compared side by side. Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

1. Character interpretation — 30 points
- Fidelity to the stated identity, age, physical presence and temperament: 15.
- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

Realism is not inherently better than stylization. Extra polygons, textures or accessories earn no credit by themselves. There is no arbitrary polygon cap or all-quad requirement. A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. The host will record any viewer limitation separately from an asset defect. An asset that cannot be opened cannot receive a visual judgment; retain its failure record without inventing a score.

These criteria are being introduced for this prompt version. Earlier attempts remain associated with the instructions they actually received.

INITIAL EXECUTION CONSTRAINTS
Work only in your own fresh workspace and create your own character independently. Do not read or reuse other benchmark entrants or other project assets. Do not invoke other models or subagents. Do not publish or start another task. Do not launch/control a browser, Playwright, native UI, mouse or keyboard, or start preview servers. No GPU/performance benchmarks on the user's computer. Create one complete, standalone 3D humanoid character from the supplied brief. Choose the art style yourself. Realistic, stylized and other coherent interpretations are welcome; no particular visual style is preferred or prescribed.

Deliver the finished character as a self-contained GLB. Embed any textures used so the asset does not depend on external image files or remote URLs. The complete character must be inspectable from the front, sides, back and above, with a modeled head, torso, arms, hands, legs and feet. Finish the asset as a whole rather than as a single-view presentation.

Use a neutral A-pose or T-pose with clear separation between the arms and torso and between the legs. The pose should make the character easy to inspect and prepare for later rigging. Express personality through the design, proportions, face and details rather than through an action pose.

Prepare the asset for a later rigging pass: keep the body parts anatomically coherent within your chosen style, avoid accidental fusions between limbs and adjacent clothing, and make the major joints identifiable. A riggable intention is not a claim that untested deformation will work perfectly. A skeleton, skin weights and animations are not required and do not earn credit in this benchmark; focus on the static character. If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Alongside the GLB, provide a short handoff identifying the file, your chosen art direction and any known limitations. Keep the final asset self-contained regardless of how it was made.

TIME LIMIT AND RUN HANDOFF

You have a hard maximum of one hour per character, measured from your actual implementation start. Record that start timestamp and the deadline exactly one hour later before beginning implementation. The hour includes asset creation, tool use, troubleshooting, checking the exported asset and final fixes. Ordinary work and tool waits do not pause the clock. Stop all implementation and asset editing by the deadline, even if the result is incomplete. Record your actual stop timestamp, disclose any interruptions and report unfinished work honestly. Do not replace actual timing evidence with an estimate.

Work independently through the attempt without mid-run coaching messages. Make your own creative and technical decisions within the brief and the existing permissions. If an action needs approval, pause that action and report the blocker; continue other permitted work within the same running time limit.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Your final handoff must identify the GLB file and include the actual implementation-start timestamp, one-hour deadline and actual stop timestamp, with the time zone stated. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Esme Duval, a 9-year-old girl who makes tiny puppet shows for her cousins. She plans elaborate stories, then changes the ending as soon as someone laughs at an unexpected part. She is confident about her ideas but shy when asked to explain them to unfamiliar adults. She wants to finish a show that gives her quieter cousin a good part instead of doing every voice herself.

Esme is sturdy and a little stocky for her age, with a rounded belly, short limbs and small broad hands. Her face is round, with full cheeks, a scattering of freckles, a small gap between her upper front teeth and a concentrated, almost-smiling expression. Her thick wavy hair has an uneven chin-length cut and one simple clip keeping it out of her eyes. Keep the head, body, joints and extremities recognizably those of a child rather than a miniature adult.

Choose ordinary, age-appropriate clothes with two visible layers, such as a soft underlayer and a firmer outer garment; the actual garments and palette are yours to decide. Include one small homemade-looking decorative detail that reflects her taste without depending on readable writing. Model hair, fabric thickness and closures intentionally, with the same care at the back as the front. No puppet, stage, toy, other person or environmental object is required. Retain the neutral inspection pose, clear limb separation and fully visible hands.

BENCHMARK PURPOSE AND GRADING CRITERIA — DRAFT V2

This is a static 3D character benchmark. The host will display your exported asset in a shared neutral inspection studio with camera and lighting controls. Different attempts at the same character brief will be compared side by side. Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

1. Character interpretation — 30 points
- Fidelity to the stated identity, age, physical presence and temperament: 15.
- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

Realism is not inherently better than stylization. Extra polygons, textures or accessories earn no credit by themselves. There is no arbitrary polygon cap or all-quad requirement. A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. The host will record any viewer limitation separately from an asset defect. An asset that cannot be opened cannot receive a visual judgment; retain its failure record without inventing a score.

These criteria are being introduced for this prompt version. Earlier attempts remain associated with the instructions they actually received.

sourceDocuments.text:
Create one complete, standalone 3D humanoid character from the supplied brief. Choose the art style yourself. Realistic, stylized and other coherent interpretations are welcome; no particular visual style is preferred or prescribed.

Deliver the finished character as a self-contained GLB. Embed any textures used so the asset does not depend on external image files or remote URLs. The complete character must be inspectable from the front, sides, back and above, with a modeled head, torso, arms, hands, legs and feet. Finish the asset as a whole rather than as a single-view presentation.

Use a neutral A-pose or T-pose with clear separation between the arms and torso and between the legs. The pose should make the character easy to inspect and prepare for later rigging. Express personality through the design, proportions, face and details rather than through an action pose.

Prepare the asset for a later rigging pass: keep the body parts anatomically coherent within your chosen style, avoid accidental fusions between limbs and adjacent clothing, and make the major joints identifiable. A riggable intention is not a claim that untested deformation will work perfectly. A skeleton, skin weights and animations are not required and do not earn credit in this benchmark; focus on the static character. If a tool supplies an existing rig or animation data with the asset, you may preserve it; no stripping or animation tests are required.

Multiple meshes are allowed. Use mesh organization and topology appropriate to your chosen approach. There is no arbitrary polygon cap and no all-quad requirement. Clothing and accessories can be separate meshes, provided the delivered character is complete and coherent. No handheld prop is required. Any optional accessories should leave the face, body and limb structure readily inspectable.

Choose the clothing, materials, palette and detailing. Treat the supplied history, temperament, age and physical presence as the character's identity, not as an exhaustive costume specification. Do not rely on written explanations, equipment or environmental objects to compensate for an unfinished character.

Deliver the character asset only. The host will provide a separate inspection studio. No environment, studio, custom lighting setup, turntable animation or presentation application is required.

Alongside the GLB, provide a short handoff identifying the file, your chosen art direction and any known limitations. Keep the final asset self-contained regardless of how it was made.

TIME LIMIT AND RUN HANDOFF

You have a hard maximum of one hour per character, measured from your actual implementation start. Record that start timestamp and the deadline exactly one hour later before beginning implementation. The hour includes asset creation, tool use, troubleshooting, checking the exported asset and final fixes. Ordinary work and tool waits do not pause the clock. Stop all implementation and asset editing by the deadline, even if the result is incomplete. Record your actual stop timestamp, disclose any interruptions and report unfinished work honestly. Do not replace actual timing evidence with an estimate.

Work independently through the attempt without mid-run coaching messages. Make your own creative and technical decisions within the brief and the existing permissions. If an action needs approval, pause that action and report the blocker; continue other permitted work within the same running time limit.

Use tools available within your existing access. Do not use paid services, create new credentials, expand permissions or communicate externally without approval. This prompt does not grant new access or authorize those actions.

Your final handoff must identify the GLB file and include the actual implementation-start timestamp, one-hour deadline and actual stop timestamp, with the time zone stated. Include your art direction, checks actually performed, known limitations and anything incomplete. Report only checks you carried out; do not claim rigging or deformation validation from a static export alone.

CHARACTER BRIEF

Create Esme Duval, a 9-year-old girl who makes tiny puppet shows for her cousins. She plans elaborate stories, then changes the ending as soon as someone laughs at an unexpected part. She is confident about her ideas but shy when asked to explain them to unfamiliar adults. She wants to finish a show that gives her quieter cousin a good part instead of doing every voice herself.

Esme is sturdy and a little stocky for her age, with a rounded belly, short limbs and small broad hands. Her face is round, with full cheeks, a scattering of freckles, a small gap between her upper front teeth and a concentrated, almost-smiling expression. Her thick wavy hair has an uneven chin-length cut and one simple clip keeping it out of her eyes. Keep the head, body, joints and extremities recognizably those of a child rather than a miniature adult.

Choose ordinary, age-appropriate clothes with two visible layers, such as a soft underlayer and a firmer outer garment; the actual garments and palette are yours to decide. Include one small homemade-looking decorative detail that reflects her taste without depending on readable writing. Model hair, fabric thickness and closures intentionally, with the same care at the back as the front. No puppet, stage, toy, other person or environmental object is required. Retain the neutral inspection pose, clear limb separation and fully visible hands.

BENCHMARK PURPOSE AND GRADING CRITERIA — DRAFT V2

This is a static 3D character benchmark. The host will display your exported asset in a shared neutral inspection studio with camera and lighting controls. Different attempts at the same character brief will be compared side by side. Overall pairwise preference is a separate judgment from the following 100-point rubric; do not optimize for an invented automatic score.

1. Character interpretation — 30 points
- Fidelity to the stated identity, age, physical presence and temperament: 15.
- Specificity and personality expressed through the model itself: 10.
- Coherence between the character's history, habits and chosen design: 5.

2. Visual execution — 45 points
- Convincing, intentional proportions and anatomy within the chosen art style: 15.
- Quality of the face, hands and other focal details: 10.
- Coherent materials, colors, surface treatment and clothing: 10.
- Consistent completeness and craftsmanship from front, sides, back and above: 10.

3. Technical quality and inspectability — 25 points
- Self-contained, structurally valid GLB that loads reliably without missing dependencies: 10.
- Clean geometry and materials without unintended gaps, broken normals, distracting intersections or accidental fusions: 10.
- Practical responsiveness and resource use in the common viewer, with well-organized scene data: 5.

Realism is not inherently better than stylization. Extra polygons, textures or accessories earn no credit by themselves. There is no arbitrary polygon cap or all-quad requirement. A skeleton, skin weights and animation earn no credit. Neutral pose and coherent joint/limb structure support static inspection and future rigging, but untested deformation is not assumed to work. Assess technical performance under equivalent host conditions; do not run prohibited performance tests during this attempt. The host will record any viewer limitation separately from an asset defect. An asset that cannot be opened cannot receive a visual judgment; retain its failure record without inventing a score.

These criteria are being introduced for this prompt version. Earlier attempts remain associated with the instructions they actually received.

INITIAL EXECUTION CONSTRAINTS
Work only in your own fresh workspace and create your own character independently. Do not read or reuse other benchmark entrants or other project assets. Do not invoke other models or subagents. Do not publish or start another task. Do not launch/control a browser, Playwright, native UI, mouse or keyboard, or start preview servers. No GPU/performance benchmarks on the user's computer. Headless asset generation and lightweight non-browser asset/export checks are permitted. Disclose visual/interactive/deformation checks not performed. Use available reputable tools within existing permissions; any blocked action stays blocked. Before your final receipt, stop all workspace-owned background/test processes and verify cleanup. Preserve the final self-contained GLB and generation source with timing, actual checks and limitations. Requested model: recorded in the launch metadata; reasoning XHIGH. Disclose if serving backend is not independently exposed. The parent will send no mid-run messages. Use the grading criteria stated above.
